# Fit for Service {-}

> "You therefore must endure hardship as a good soldier of Christ Jesus. No soldier on duty entangles himself in the affairs of life, that he may please him who enrolled him as a soldier."
>
> — 2 Timothy 2:3-4

Before the final step, one short chapter. It has no number, because it isn't part of the method. It is about what you are being set free for.

## Who gains? {-}

Here is a question this book has kept back until now. Who gains from your habit?

You don't. So who does? There are companies that earn more the longer you stay aroused, alone and tired. Something does better when men are numb and spent. A Christian has a name for that something, and Peter warned the people he loved about him: "Your adversary, the devil, walks around like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour." If you don't believe in a devil, call it a business model. It is working on you either way.

And it never has to fight you. Here is a man with people to love and work to do. Perhaps he has something to build that would do some good in the world. How do you stop him? Show him a little skin on a screen and he takes himself off the field. Twenty minutes later he is spent, and no use to anybody until tomorrow. Tomorrow you can do it again. It's the cheapest victory there is.

None of that is an excuse. The apostle James won't let a man say the devil made him do it: "each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed." The bait is dangled, but the appetite is yours. That is good news, because it means the way out is yours as well.

Now think what all this says about you. Nobody bothers to distract a man who doesn't matter. You were worth taking out of the fight.

## The king on the roof {-}

Scripture has the case study. "At the return of the year, at the time when kings go out, David sent Joab, and his servants with him, and all Israel ... But David stayed at Jerusalem. At evening, David arose from his bed and walked on the roof of the king's house. From the roof, he saw a woman bathing, and the woman was very beautiful to look at."

This was the man who killed Goliath. No army ever beat him in the field. He was beaten on a rooftop on an idle evening, at the time when kings go out, because he hadn't gone.

Don't read it as a story about a beautiful woman. Her name was Bathsheba, and the king sent men to fetch her. Nobody asked what she wanted. She became pregnant. Her husband, Uriah, was one of David's best soldiers, and he was away at the front. David called him home and "made him drunk", hoping he would go to his wife and cover the thing up. Uriah wouldn't take a comfort that his friends in the field couldn't have. So David sent him back to the war carrying a letter to his commander, and the letter got him killed.

It began with one look on an idle evening. A woman was used, a good man was buried, and a child died. Lust told David it was private. It never is. Somebody else always pays.

## Drunk on duty {-}

Now let me say this plainly, without taking back the promise that nobody here will shame you.

You may be a Christian. You may be on God's side, and he does love you. "There is therefore now no condemnation" was true in the Introduction, and it is true on this page. And you were made on purpose. Paul says the work was planned as well as the man: "we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them." There is something with your name on it that nobody else is placed to do.

But a man ruled by lust is like a soldier who turns up drunk for duty. He is loved, he is enlisted, and he is unfit for service. He can't fight at full strength, and the people counting on him get less than the whole of him. You know who they are. Paul names the two things in one breath: "since we belong to the day, let's be sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love, and for a helmet, the hope of salvation." Sober comes first, and then the armour.

So get the order right. The people who know most about getting sober learned this the hard way. One of their earliest handbooks says it flatly: "Sobriety is the most important thing in your life, without exception." Whatever you put ahead of it, they say, you will lose. First doesn't mean building your life around it. It means settling it, so that you can get on with everything else. A sober soldier doesn't spend the day thinking about drink. He does his job.

Now the good news, which is the reason this book exists. This is not hard to settle. Nobody is sending you on a ten-year campaign. You've read twenty-six chapters and you know what the thing is: a trick, an itch that feeds itself, a lie about comfort. It doesn't take courage to put down a thing you have seen through.

And being fit is not the price of being loved. It is what a loved man is for.

If you're not a believer, keep the picture and change the flag. You still have people who depend on you and work that is yours to do, and you have been turning up to both half-present. The order of things is the same for you.

When Isaiah heard the question, "Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?", he had just been forgiven, and he made no speech about his record. He said, "Here I am. Send me!"

The next chapter is where you say it.
